chapter_title: Interacting with Smart Contracts using Ethers.js and Hardhat Runtime Environment

screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contracts
screens.subtitle: Ethers.js fundamentals and the Hardhat Runtime Environment for deploy & interaction

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how to move from compiled contracts to real interactions. We focus on the Ethers. js library and the Hardhat Runtime Environment as your primary tools. You will understand three core Ethers. js abstractions — Providers, Signers, and Contract instances — and how Hardhat injects a pre-configured ethers object so scripts are concise and safe. We will walk through a full deployment script, show how to call a read-only view function, and how to send a state-changing transaction while correctly waiting for confirmation. You will also see common pitfalls, like reading state before a transaction is mined, and practical safety advice about private keys and local networks. By the end you will be able to write a Hardhat script that deploys MyContract, calls greeting, updates it, and verifies the change. This matters because reliable interaction is essential for testing, automation, and for building front-end integrations. As you explore, notice the pattern: read with Providers, sign with Signers, and operate with Contract objects. Think about one place you might use a read-only provider versus a signer when building a small dApp.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use Ethers.js with Hardhat's HRE to read blockchain state with Providers, send signed transactions with Signers, and interact via Contract instances. Always wait for tx confirmations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will complete four practical objectives that turn compiled contracts into interactive instances. First, you will explain why Ethers. js is the recommended library for JavaScript interactions with Ethereum, including how it balances compact A P I design with secure wallet handling. Second, you will distinguish Providers, Signers, and Contract instances and name the role each plays in read versus write operations, which matters when building front-end or script-based workflows. Third, you will author a Hardhat script that deploys a contract to a local network, observing the deployment address and confirming the contract's deployed state. Fourth, you will programmatically call both view functions and state-changing functions, learning to await transaction confirmations to avoid race conditions. Each objective connects to a competency milestone so you can verify your results in a local Hardhat node. These skills are foundational for testing, automation, and safe development workflows in Ethereum projects.

screens.title: What is Ethers.js?
screens.subtitle: A compact JavaScript library to interact with Ethereum and smart contracts

narration.text: Ethers. js is a focused JavaScript library that provides the primitives you need to read blockchain state, manage wallets, and send transactions. It is created to be compact and secure, which is why it is widely used in both scripts and front-end dApps. Practically, you use Ethers. js to construct Providers that query the network, create Signers that authorize transactions, and build Contract objects that map a contract's ABI to callable JavaScript methods. For example, when you want to display a contract's public greeting on a webpage you use a Provider and a Contract instance to call the view function; no signing is required. When a user clicks a button to update that greeting, a Signer is required to sign and submit the transaction. A common misconception is that Ethers. js itself stores private keys; instead it provides Wallet objects that can hold keys in memory or connect to external signers like MetaMask. Why this matters: choosing Ethers. js keeps your scripts small and readable, and the same patterns you learn in Hardhat scripts transfer directly to browser integrations. Try to think of Providers as the eyes, Signers as the hands, and Contract instances as the interface that ties them together.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Ethers.js provides concise APIs for Providers, Signers, and Contract objects to read and write on Ethereum.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is Ethers.js?
Definition & purpose

Ethers.js is a JavaScript library for interacting with Ethereum. It focuses on clarity and security for both scripts and browser-based dApps.

Provider
Read-only network interface to fetch blocks and call view functions.
Signer / Wallet
Holds keys or connects to MetaMask to sign transactions that change state.
Contract
An ABI-bound object that exposes contract functions as methods.
Key Takeaway

Ethers.js unifies reading and writing interactions using clear abstractions you will use throughout this chapter.

Concrete example

To show a greeting on a page you might create a Provider and a Contract. For a user action that updates the greeting, you would obtain a Signer and call the contract method which returns a transaction object to await.

Analogy
Provider = eyes, Signer = hands, Contract = appliance with buttons. Eyes can read the state; hands must press the buttons to change it.
Common mistake
Confusing a Provider for a Signer and attempting to send a transaction with no signing authority.

screens.title: Providers: read-only connections
screens.subtitle: How Providers let your code query blockchain state without signing

narration.text: A Provider is Ethers. js's read-only connection to an Ethereum network. It fetches blockchain data like block numbers, transaction receipts, and return values from view functions. Providers do not hold private keys and cannot sign transactions. In practice you will choose a Provider based on the environment: JsonRpcProvider for a local Hardhat Network or Ganache, and a service-backed Provider like Infura when connecting to public networks. For example, when you want to display MyContract's greeting in a dashboard, a Provider plus a Contract instance is sufficient because the greeting() function is a view and does not require gas or a signature. A common misconception is assuming a Provider can submit transactions; it cannot. Another misconception is that all Providers behave identically; public providers may have rate limits and different latency characteristics. When writing scripts in Hardhat, prefer the HRE-injected ethers provider since it is configured for the selected network. Thinking about Providers first keeps your read paths simple and safe. Providers: read-only connections means providers fetch state and handle read-only calls. choose a provider type suited to your environment.. In practical terms, how providers let your code query blockchain state without signing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Provider role
keyIdea.text: Providers fetch state and handle read-only calls. Choose a provider type suited to your environment.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Providers: read-only connections
Provider essentials

Providers let you call view functions and query network state without signing. They are ideal for dashboards and read-only scripts.

JsonRpcProvider
Connects to a local node such as Hardhat Network; useful for development and testing.
Infura / Public providers
Connect to public networks, but be aware of rate limits and configuration differences.
Misconception
A Provider cannot sign transactions. Attempting to submit a state change without a Signer will fail.
Example scenario

In a Hardhat script you can rely on the HRE-injected provider to call greeting() on your deployed contract. The call returns the string immediately and does not cost gas.

// Example: read-only call (conceptual)
const provider = hre.ethers.provider; // injected by Hardhat
const contract = new hre.ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider);
const message = await contract.greeting();
console.log(message);
Key takeaway

Use Providers for reads and the HRE provider during local scripting for convenience and correct network targeting.

screens.title: Signers: authorizing state changes
screens.subtitle: What a Signer represents and where it appears in scripts and browsers

narration.text: A Signer is Ethers. js's representation of an account capable of signing transactions and messages. In the browser, a wallet like MetaMask acts as a Signer and exposes an interface that Ethers. js can use. In backend scripts or Hardhat tasks, a Wallet instance initialized with a private key acts as a Signer. The Signer attaches to a Contract instance when you need to execute a state-changing function, such as setGreeting, which modifies the blockchain. When you call a mutating method using a Signer, Ethers. js returns a transaction response object immediately. The actual state change happens only after the transaction is mined, so you must await the returned tx. wait() to ensure confirmation. A frequent mistake is to assume that calling a mutating function returns the new state; it returns a transaction object, not a direct value. Another nuance is that Signers are tied to accounts; careful key management and never hardcoding secrets remain essential for safety. In development, Hardhat provides pre-funded accounts that are convenient for testing. Understand Signers as the authority that converts intent to signed transactions.

keyIdea.title: Signer role
keyIdea.text: Signers hold authority to sign transactions. Use wallets in the browser or Wallet instances in scripts to send state-changing transactions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Signers: authorizing state changes
What a Signer is

A Signer represents an account that can sign transactions. It is required to modify blockchain state.

Browser Signer
MetaMask injects a web signer that Ethers.js can use for user-initiated transactions.
Script Signer
A Wallet with a private key used in backend or Hardhat scripts to sign transactions programmatically.
Misconception
Calling a state-changing method returns a tx response, not the updated value. You must wait for the transaction to be mined to read the new state.
Concrete example

In a Hardhat script you often destructure the first signer: const [deployer] = await hre.ethers.getSigners(); then use deployer when deploying or sending transactions.

Key takeaway

Treat Signers as the entity that turns your intent into signed transactions; manage private keys securely and avoid hardcoding them.

screens.title: Contract Instances: ABI, address, and methods
screens.subtitle: How Contract objects make smart contract functions accessible from JavaScript

narration.text: A Contract instance in Ethers. js binds a contract's ABI and deployed address to a Provider or Signer, exposing the contract's functions as JavaScript methods. You create one by supplying the contract address, ABI, and either a Provider for read-only calls or a Signer for sending transactions. For example, after deploying MyContract you can write const myContract = new hre. ethers. Contract(address, abi, signerOrProvider). If you attach a Provider, calls to view functions like greeting() return values immediately without gas. If you attach a Signer, invoking setGreeting will produce a transaction response that you must wait to be mined. A useful pattern is to create a read-only contract for UI rendering and a signer-bound contract for user actions. Mistakes often occur when you instantiate a contract with a Provider but then try to call a mutating method, which fails because there is no signing authority. Remember: the Contract object is the bridge between JavaScript and the on-chain code, and how you instantiate it controls whether you can only read or also write. Contract Instances: ABI, address, and methods means a contract object maps abi and address to callable methods; choose a provider or signer depending on read or write needs.. In practical terms, how contract objects make smart contract functions accessible from javascript. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contract instance
keyIdea.text: A Contract object maps ABI and address to callable methods; choose a Provider or Signer depending on read or write needs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Contract Instances
What a Contract binds
  • ABI: the function and event signatures the contract exposes.
  • Address: where the contract lives on the chosen network.
  • Provider or Signer: determines whether calls are read-only or signed transactions.
Pattern
Keep a provider-bound contract for UI reads and a signer-bound contract for writes to avoid accidental failures and reduce risk.
Concrete example

After deploying, instantiate: const myContract = await MyContract.deploy(...); or new hre.ethers.Contract(address, abi, signer). Then call await myContract.greeting() for reads or const tx = await myContract.setGreeting('Hi'); await tx.wait(); for writes.

Key takeaway

How you instantiate a Contract controls whether you can only read or also write. Pick the correct binding for the task.

screens.title: Hardhat Runtime Environment (HRE)
screens.subtitle: How Hardhat injects a configured ethers object to simplify scripts

narration.text: The Hardhat Runtime Environment, or HRE, is the global object Hardhat provides inside scripts and tasks. It bundles functionality like the configured ethers instance, network configuration, and utilities for compilation and deployments. The convenience here is that you rarely need to manually construct Providers or Signers when using the injected ethers. For example, using hre. ethers. getContractFactory will return a ContractFactory configured for the chosen network, and hre. ethers. getSigners() returns pre-configured Signer objects representing available accounts. This reduces boilerplate and helps avoid mismatches between your provider configuration and the network you intend to run on. A common misconception is thinking HRE is required outside Hardhat; HRE exists only inside Hardhat scripts and tests. When you run npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js the HRE is available automatically. Understanding HRE saves you time: it allows you to focus on contract logic rather than setting up connections. Consider HRE an orchestrator that wires Ethers. js to your project configuration. Hardhat Runtime Environment (HRE) means hre provides a pre-configured ethers object and utilities so scripts use the correct network and accounts without manual setup.. In practical terms, how hardhat injects a configured ethers object to simplify scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: HRE role
keyIdea.text: HRE provides a pre-configured ethers object and utilities so scripts use the correct network and accounts without manual setup.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Hardhat Runtime Environment (HRE)
What HRE contains
  • Configured ethers object for current network.
  • Network helpers and account access via getSigners.
  • Utilities for task and script management.
Benefit
Less configuration boilerplate and fewer mistakes connecting to the wrong network or provider.
Quick code pattern
// In scripts/deploy.js
const hre = require("hardhat");
const MyContract = await hre.ethers.getContractFactory("MyContract");
const [deployer] = await hre.ethers.getSigners();
Key takeaway

Use HRE to avoid manual provider and signer construction when scripting with Hardhat; it wires configuration for you.

screens.title: ContractFactory & Deploying
screens.subtitle: From ContractFactory to deployed instance — the deployment steps

narration.text: Deploying a contract in Hardhat follows a clear pattern centered on the ContractFactory abstraction. A ContractFactory is a blueprint for deploying instances of a specific contract. In a script you typically call hre. ethers. getContractFactory with the contract name to obtain the factory. Next, obtain a Signer — often the first available deployer account from hre. ethers. getSigners. Then call factory. deploy with constructor arguments; this returns a contract instance or a deployment transaction depending on context. Await contract. deployed() to ensure the deployment transaction is mined and the address is available. The sequence matters: skipping await contract. deployed() can cause subsequent interactions to fail because the network has not yet included the deployment transaction. A concrete example is deploying MyContract with an initial greeting string. After deploying and awaiting deployment, you will have myContract. address to use for later interactions. Treat ContractFactory as the standard way to create on-chain contract instances programmatically. ContractFactory & Deploying means use getcontractfactory, getsigners, factory.deploy(...), then await contract.deployed() to ensure confirmation and a usable address.. In practical terms, from contractfactory to deployed instance — the deployment steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment pattern
keyIdea.text: Use getContractFactory, getSigners, factory.deploy(...), then await contract.deployed() to ensure confirmation and a usable address.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › ContractFactory & Deploying
Steps to deploy
  1. Get ContractFactory: const MyContract = await hre.ethers.getContractFactory('MyContract');
  2. Get deployer: const [deployer] = await hre.ethers.getSigners();
  3. Deploy: const myContract = await MyContract.deploy('Hello');
  4. Await confirmation: await myContract.deployed(); then read myContract.address.
Warning
Omitting await myContract.deployed() may cause later calls to fail because the contract address is not yet confirmed on chain.
Example — initial greeting

Deploy MyContract with an initial message, then log the address. This address is used to construct Contract instances for later reads and writes.

// Deploy pattern (visual)
const MyContract = await hre.ethers.getContractFactory("MyContract");
const [deployer] = await hre.ethers.getSigners();
const myContract = await MyContract.deploy("Hello, Cohortia!");
await myContract.deployed();
console.log("MyContract deployed to:", myContract.address);
Key takeaway

Follow the factory → deploy → deployed pattern to obtain a confirmed deployed contract address for further interactions.

screens.title: Walkthrough: scripts/deploy.js
screens.subtitle: Step through a full Hardhat deploy and interaction script

narration.text: Let's walk through a complete deployment and interaction script line by line so you internalize the pattern. The script begins by requiring the Hardhat environment, which gives access to hre. ethers. Then it gets the ContractFactory for MyContract; the factory is used to create a deployed instance. Next it fetches available signers and selects the first as deployer; this is the account that will authorize the deployment transaction. Deploy is called with an initial greeting argument, which returns a contract object. Awaiting contract. deployed() is necessary to wait for the transaction to be mined and to get a stable address. After deployment, the script calls a view function greeting() which returns the current string and is free to call. To change the greeting, the script calls setGreeting which returns a transaction response object; the code then awaits tx. wait() to ensure the transaction is mined before calling greeting() again to verify the new value. A common mistake is to omit await tx. wait() and immediately read the state, which will return the old value. This walkthrough demonstrates the end-to-end lifecycle of deployment, read, write, and verification.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: The deploy script shows getContractFactory, getSigners, deploy, deployed, view calls, state changes, and the necessity of awaiting tx.wait().

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Walkthrough: scripts/deploy.js
Full script (from source)
// scripts/deploy.js
const hre = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const MyContract = await hre.ethers.getContractFactory("MyContract");
  const [deployer] = await hre.ethers.getSigners();
  console.log("Deploying contract with the account:", deployer.address);

  const myContract = await MyContract.deploy("Hello, Cohortia!");
  await myContract.deployed();
  console.log("MyContract deployed to:", myContract.address);

  let currentGreeting = await myContract.greeting();
  console.log("Current greeting:", currentGreeting);

  const tx = await myContract.setGreeting("Greetings from Hardhat!");
  await tx.wait();

  currentGreeting = await myContract.greeting();
  console.log("New greeting:", currentGreeting);
}

main().then(() => process.exit(0)).catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1); });
Explanation & callouts
  • Require Hardhat to access hre and the injected ethers instance.
  • getContractFactory returns the deployment blueprint for MyContract.
  • getSigners gives accounts; the deployer signs the deployment transaction.
  • Await deployed() to ensure the address is confirmed before using it.
  • Call greeting() for a view; call setGreeting() to change state and await tx.wait() to confirm.
Common mistake
Reading state immediately after a mutating call without awaiting tx.wait() leads to stale values.
Try this

Run npx hardhat node in a separate terminal, then npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js and watch the printed greetings change.

screens.title: View vs State-Changing Functions
screens.subtitle: Understand free reads versus gas-costing transactions with examples

narration.text: Smart contract functions fall into two practical categories: view (read-only) and state-changing (write) functions. A view function, such as greeting() in MyContract, only reads contract state and does not alter the blockchain. Calling a view function is typically free and does not require a Signer; a Provider and a Contract instance are enough. A state-changing function, like setGreeting, modifies storage and therefore requires a transaction signed by a Signer, consumes gas, and results in a transaction response that must be mined. Consider the greeting example: calling greeting() returns the current string immediately, while calling setGreeting requires sending a transaction and waiting for that transaction to be included in a block. A common misunderstanding is to expect immediate state changes; because mining takes time, you must await tx. wait() before reading the updated state. In practice, design your UI to show pending transaction status and then refresh state after confirmation. This contrast is central to building responsive, correct dApps and scripts. View vs State-Changing Functions means view functions read state without gas; state-changing functions require signed transactions, gas, and confirmation via tx.wait().. In practical terms, understand free reads versus gas-costing transactions with examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Read vs Write
keyIdea.text: View functions read state without gas; state-changing functions require signed transactions, gas, and confirmation via tx.wait().

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › View vs State-Changing Functions
View (read-only)

No gas, no signature required. Use smells like greeting(). Good for dashboards and frequent reads.

Example
const msg = await myContract.greeting(); // returns string immediately
State-changing (write)

Requires a Signer, costs gas, returns a transaction response that must be mined before state changes are visible.

Example
const tx = await myContract.setGreeting('Hi'); await tx.wait(); // wait for confirmation
Tip for UI
Show transaction pending state after sending a transaction and refresh view data only after tx.wait() completes to avoid showing stale state.

screens.title: Transactions and tx.wait()
screens.subtitle: Why awaiting confirmations matters and how to do it correctly

narration.text: When you send a state-changing transaction with Ethers. js you receive a transaction response immediately, but the blockchain state changes only when the transaction is mined. The method tx. wait() is the correct way to pause your script until the transaction is included in a block and confirmed. Forgetting to call await tx. wait() leads to race conditions where subsequent reads still return old values. In automated scripts this manifests as tests that intermittently fail or as UI displays that do not reflect the intended update. The pattern is straightforward: const tx = await contract. setSomething(...); await tx. wait(); then call the read function to verify. For local Hardhat Network runs, confirmations are usually quick, but tx. wait() is still necessary for deterministic behavior. Also be mindful of waiting for multiple confirmations in production contexts if you need stronger finality; in local development a single confirmation is sufficient. Always treat the transaction response as a promise of a future state change, not the final result itself. Transactions and tx.wait() means use await tx.wait() after sending transactions to ensure the state change is mined and visible for subsequent reads or steps.. In practical terms, why awaiting confirmations matters and how to do it correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Await confirmations
keyIdea.text: Use await tx.wait() after sending transactions to ensure the state change is mined and visible for subsequent reads or steps.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Transactions and tx.wait()
Why tx.wait() matters

tx.wait() waits for the transaction to be mined so later reads show the updated state. Treat the transaction response as a promise of state change, not its completion.

// Correct pattern
const tx = await myContract.setGreeting('New');
await tx.wait();
const updated = await myContract.greeting();
Common mistake
Not awaiting tx.wait() and immediately reading state results in stale values and confusing errors in automation.
Practical guidance
  • Always await tx.wait() in scripts and tests to ensure deterministic results.
  • Show transaction pending and confirmation UI to users to avoid confusion.
  • In production consider waiting for multiple confirmations if higher finality is required.
Key takeaway

Make tx.wait() a standard step after sending transactions to secure predictable behavior.

screens.title: Run the hands-on activity
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: compile, run a local node, deploy, and interact

narration.text: This hands-on activity consolidates everything you've learned. First, ensure your Hardhat project is set up and MyContract. sol exists in the contracts folder. Compile your contracts using npx hardhat compile. Next, start a local Hardhat Network with npx hardhat node in a separate terminal; this provides pre-funded accounts and a deterministic environment. Then create scripts/deploy. js with the deploy-and-interact code provided in the chapter. Run the script against the running node using npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js. Observe the printed deployer address, the deployed contract address, and the greeting values before and after setGreeting. If you modify the script to set a third greeting and verify it, you'll practice chaining multiple transactions and using await tx. wait() for each. A recommended challenge is adding an extra call to setGreeting and reading back the final greeting. As you work, remember not to hardcode real private keys and to use environment variables if you need to test with a custom signer. Run the hands-on activity means compile, run npx hardhat node, run deploy script, observe outputs, and extend the script with an additional setgreeting call to verify chaining and tx.wait().. In practical terms, step-by-step: compile, run a local node, deploy, and interact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Follow these steps in separate terminals as described to verify the full flow.
